title: Cannabis laws could make insurance high
full_text:
The Premier’s overhaul of drug driving laws could push up the cost of green slips, with the government conceding it has no idea whether a three-strikes warning system for medical cannabis patients will impact Compulsory Third Party insurance costs.
The Daily Telegraph can also reveal that digital drivers’ licences would identify motorists who have opted into the cannabis driving register, by displaying patients’ prescription status.
The drug driving overhaul was on Thursday set to go to a final vote in the Upper House, with Labor having the numbers to pass the legislation.
But ahead of the vote, Transport Minister John Graham conceded that “no modelling of cost impacts on car insurance of the reforms has been conducted”.
Labor’s legislation would let registered medical cannabis users escape without penalty for driving with more than 50 nanograms of THC in their system.
Cannabis patients would undergo the existing roadside drug testing process, but would be given two warnings if they tested over the existing threshold. The Minns government pushed the legislation through parliament in the face of opposition from the Coalition and trauma doctors, who warned it would cost lives.
Liberal Transport spokeswoman Natalie Ward questioned why the government did no modelling on what the overhaul would mean for family budgets.
“The Premier’s three-strikes policy for medicinal cannabis users getting caught drug driving won’t make our roads safer – who is going to foot the bill if insurers jack up their prices?” she asked.
She said Premier Chris Minns should “come out and guarantee that insurers won’t hike CTP prices because of this overhaul”.
The Insurance Council of Australia could not say what impact the law changes would have on premiums.
“Any implications for insurance premiums will depend on a range of factors and cannot be determined at this stage,” an ICA spokeswoman said. “Insurers will continue to assess available data and evidence as it emerges.” Meanwhile, the Telegraph can also reveal that cannabis patients who opt into the drug-driving warning scheme will have their medical details displayed on their digital drivers’ licence.
A discrete “licence condition” displayed on the digital licence will reveal whether someone has a prescription for medicinal marijuana.
Patients would be recorded in the Transport for NSW “DRIVES” database. Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said access to the “medicinal cannabis patient register” would be limited, to safeguard patient safety.
“Access to the patient register will be configured so users only see the information necessary for their role.” Royal North Shore Hospital Director of Trauma Services Dr Geoff Healy was one of a number of doctors who wrote to Mr Minns urging him to ditch the legislation. “I really fear for our general population that they’re going to be put at increased risk,” Dr Healy said.
